question: Can finite-step and minibatch effects be represented as an effective entropic loss whose symmetry breaking predicts gradient balance, representation alignment, and whether SGD selects sharp or flat solutions?

key_findings.claim: A backward-error expansion turns one finite learning-rate update into gradient flow on a modified, data-averaged loss through first or second order in the step matrix.
key_findings.evidence: Theorem 1 adds a first-order squared minibatch-gradient term and a Hessian-dependent second-order term, with explicit local approximation errors. Equation 3 then averages the leading correction and weight decay into the effective loss used by later theorems.

key_findings.claim: For exponential rescaling symmetries, stationary points of the leading effective loss obey gradient-noise balance conditions across layers, neurons, and factored matrices.
key_findings.evidence: The master-balance theorem contracts the symmetry generator with minibatch-gradient second moments and weight norms. Specializations yield layer and neuron equipartition and key/query-style matrix alignment; teacher-student linear, ReLU, and attention experiments show the balance residuals decreasing with the effective entropy.

key_findings.claim: The claimed perfect Platonic representation result is exact only for global optima of a broad-width embedded deep linear model in a limiting regime.
key_findings.evidence: Theorem 8 proves every hidden-layer pair differs only by scale and rotation under invertible input/output transforms, zero weight decay, and the leading entropic-loss limit. Nonlinear teacher-student and pretrained ViT comparisons are supportive correlations, not an extension of the theorem to arbitrary deep models.

key_findings.claim: In a two-layer linear regression model, anisotropic label noise can make the entropically selected solution arbitrarily sharper than the minimum-sharpness factorization.
key_findings.evidence: Theorem 10 gives total sharpness as a function of input and label-noise covariances. For identity signal/input covariance, imbalance in the label-noise spectrum makes the expression diverge, while isotropic label noise recovers the minimal sharpness; simulations vary noise balance and reproduce flattening or sharpening phases.

method.core_idea: Use backward-error analysis to define a leading effective loss for finite-step stochastic gradients, then exploit parameter symmetries to derive equilibrium constraints and solve representative linear models.
method.mechanism: The gradient-fluctuation correction breaks non-orthogonal continuous symmetries while preserving orthogonal discrete ones. Differentiating along exponential symmetry orbits produces balance equations; solving them selects particular factorizations from functionally equivalent minima.
assumptions: The learning rate is sufficiently small for the truncated effective-loss expansion to approximate the discrete stochastic dynamics.
The relevant models have exact exponential parameter symmetries and reach local or global minima of the leading effective loss.
Minibatch sampling and, for most theorems, a scalar fixed learning rate capture the optimizer's implicit force.

techniques.role: Approximates discrete SGD by continuous flow on a learning-rate-dependent modified objective.
Differentiates the effective loss along scale-equivalent parameterizations to derive noise/weight equipartition.
Solves idealized deep-linear global optima to make representation and sharpness predictions exact.

evaluations.setting: Teacher-student linear, ReLU, and simple self-attention networks on MNIST-like data
evaluations.metric: Layer/neuron gradient-balance residual versus effective entropy
evaluations.result: Balance residuals decline during training and correlate with the entropy term more than the task loss.
evaluations.baseline: Ordinary weight balance and task-loss trajectory.

evaluations.setting: Two independently trained six-layer linear or tanh networks on transformed MNIST
evaluations.result: Every layer pair becomes strongly or, for the linear setting, nearly perfectly aligned despite transformed inputs.
evaluations.baseline: Alignment to raw inputs and arbitrary unbalanced global-minimum factorizations.

evaluations.metric: Representational alignment across MLP and attention layers
evaluations.result: Later layers and within-model pairs align more strongly, with positive cross-model alignment.

evaluations.setting: Two-layer linear regression with controlled anisotropic label noise
evaluations.metric: Learning-rate-scaled largest eigenvalue and total sharpness
evaluations.result: More balanced noise yields lower sharpness and better stability, consistent with the closed form.

limitations: Author-stated: the theory assumes explicit exact symmetries and focuses on leading-order corrections; approximate symmetries and higher-order finite-step effects remain open.
Author-stated: code is not released; experiments are presented as small demonstrations.
Reviewer inference: calling the correction entropy is an analogy—the defined quantity is a gradient-second-moment regularizer, not thermodynamic state entropy.

Reviewer inference: the exact universal-representation claim does not cover nonlinear frontier models, adaptive time-varying preconditioners, nonstationary data, or optimization away from global minima.
failure_modes: At large learning rates, neglected higher-order terms can dominate and reverse leading-order sharpness predictions, as the authors note for a late training phase.
Adam-like matrix preconditioning can break even orthogonal invariances retained by scalar SGD, changing the selected equilibrium.
Weight decay trades gradient balance for weight balance and can destroy the exact alignment solution.
reusable_insights: Analyze an optimizer's selected parameterization, not only the function-level loss, when symmetry creates continua of equivalent minima.
Gradient-noise second moments can furnish measurable equilibrium conditions across rescaling-equivalent modules.
Any universal-representation theorem should state the equivalence class—rotation, scale, and input transforms—and the regime in which alignment is exact.
open_questions: Can the balance laws be made nonasymptotic for time-varying Adam preconditioners and momentum?
Which approximate symmetries yield quantitatively stable near-balance predictions in transformers?
Does entropic alignment predict causal feature interchangeability or only representational similarity?

competitive_landscape.title: Parameter Symmetry and Noise Equilibrium of Stochastic Gradient Descent
competitive_landscape.difference: Ziyin et al. derive Noether flow and noise equilibria along exponential symmetries; Neural Thermodynamics recasts that motion as an effective-loss force and extends it to Platonic alignment and sharpness formulas.

competitive_landscape.title: Implicit Gradient Regularization
competitive_landscape.difference: Barrett and Dherin derive finite-step implicit gradient regularization; the reviewed work generalizes the correction to stochastic/matrix steps and centers symmetry breaking and representation selection.

competitive_landscape.title: Stochastic Collapse: How Gradient Noise Attracts SGD Dynamics Towards Simpler Subnetworks
competitive_landscape.difference: Stochastic Collapse analyzes noise-driven attraction toward simpler subnetworks; this paper derives symmetry-orbit balance from an effective loss and targets aligned factorizations rather than subnetworks.

competitive_landscape.title: The Platonic Representation Hypothesis
competitive_landscape.difference: Huh et al. document empirical convergence and propose capacity, simplicity, and task pressures; the reviewed work proves rotation-and-scale alignment in an embedded deep-linear model via SGD's symmetry-breaking selection.

novelty_assessment: Author claim: a rigorous entropic-force formalism unifies gradient equipartition, universal representations, and opposing sharpness trends. Reviewer inference after primary-source comparison: modified-loss and symmetry/noise-equilibrium ingredients predate the paper, including closely related work by the same group; the novel value is their synthesis and the exact deep-linear alignment/sharpness applications, whose scope is substantially narrower than the universal rhetoric.
reviewer_notes: Read all thirty-three extracted pages, including full theorem proofs, experimental appendices, limitations, and checklist. I distinguish exact statements for the truncated effective loss/deep-linear models from suggestive nonlinear and ViT evidence. Competitor records were checked on primary arXiv pages on 2026-08-23.
